takeaways: Discounted office keeps trading: 601W Cos. is closing on the ground lease at BXP's 7 Times Square for roughly $700M (~$580/sf) — half the $1,150/sf mark set when Norges bought in at a $1.5B valuation in 2013.

Senior housing remains the strongest fundamentals story in CRE. Welltower raised 2026 same-store senior housing NOI growth guidance to 18.5%–21.5% on occupancy up 330 bps to 89.4%, and roughly half of Ventas's 807 communities now sit at or above 90%.

Debt is the pressure point. The Fed held at 3.50%–3.75% on July 29 with three dissents favoring a hike, commercial mortgage rates start at 5.70%, and ~$1 trillion of loans matures in 2026 as apartment CMBS delinquencies hit a nine-year high.

items.headline: 601W nears $700M deal for BXP's 7 Times Square ground lease
items.summary: 601W Cos. (Mark Karasick, Victor Gerstein, Michael Silberberg, with Harry Skydell leading) is finalizing a purchase of the ground lease on 7 Times Square, the 1.2M sf Manhattan tower BXP began shopping via Eastdil in May at about $700M, or ~$580/sf. That is a steep haircut from 2013, when Norges Bank paid $684M for a 45% stake at a $1.5B valuation ($1,150/sf). Tenants include KnitWell, Snowflake and several law firms; 60-plus years remain on the city ground lease. (via The Promote)

items.headline: Welltower raises 2026 senior housing NOI guidance to 18.5%–21.5%
items.summary: Welltower posted Q2 2026 EPS of $1.60 versus $0.64 expected on revenue of $3.54B, up 39.1% year over year. Same-store senior housing occupancy rose 330 bps to 89.4% with RevPOR growth of 5.2% against expense growth per room of just 0.7%. The REIT also closed the 38-community Amica Senior Lifestyles portfolio for $1.91B while shedding $7.2B of outpatient medical assets — a clear signal of where institutional capital sees the best risk-adjusted returns.

items.headline: Ventas CIO: rising occupancy means senior living must evolve past 'old standard'
items.summary: Ventas CIO John Hutchens says about half of the REIT's 807 same-store senior housing communities are at or above 90% occupancy, and another 10% are approaching 100%. With census climbing toward practical capacity, the growth lever shifts from lease-up to rate, program differentiation and operating margin. For Lloyd Jones, this argues for pushing RevPOR and resident experience investment now rather than waiting for occupancy tailwinds.

items.headline: CMBS distress concentrates in a handful of top U.S. metros
items.summary: Commercial Observer's August analysis maps where CMBS distress is clustering, with office delinquencies having pushed to a record 12.3% by January 2026 and the overall Trepp delinquency rate at 7.55% in May. Distress is not evenly distributed — a small set of gateway and high-supply metros carry a disproportionate share. Operators refinancing in 2026 should expect lender pricing to reflect metro-level distress data, not just asset performance.

items.headline: Apartment CMBS delinquencies hit nine-year high as distress sales stay slow
items.summary: Trepp data show multifamily CMBS delinquencies at their highest level in nine years, with special servicing rates climbing even as distressed sales volume remains muted — a sign owners and lenders are still extending rather than transacting. Recent newly delinquent loans include $61M on Ariza Forest View in Santa Rosa Beach, FL and $53.1M on Mirasol in Las Vegas. The gap between distress on paper and distress in the market is where 2026 acquisition opportunities will emerge.

items.headline: Fed holds at 3.50%–3.75% with three dissents; CRE rates start at 5.70%
items.summary: The FOMC held the funds rate steady on July 29 with three regional presidents dissenting in favor of a hike, and Chair Kevin Warsh signaled no hesitation to fight inflation — markets now price little chance of near-term cuts. As of August 10, multifamily loans over $6M start at 5.70%, apartment loans under $6M at 6.11%, CMBS at 6.63% and SBA 504 at 6.03%. With nearly $1 trillion maturing in 2026, refinancing math stays tight.

items.headline: AI push puts CRE on track for a $605 billion investment year
items.summary: Commercial real estate investment is pacing toward roughly $605 billion in 2026, a 16% jump over 2025, driven substantially by AI-related data center and infrastructure demand. About 80% of data center capacity under development is expected to be leased before it opens. The capital crowding into digital infrastructure is a competing bid for the same institutional dollars chasing senior housing and multifamily.

items.headline: AvalonBay–Equity Residential $71B merger gets a cool market reception
items.summary: The roughly $71B AVB–EQR multifamily mega-merger is drawing skepticism from investors, with JLL Income Property Trust's Allan Swaringen conceding that 'the market has not piled into [AVB-EQR].' The Promote frames the tie-up as a marriage of convenience rather than a growth story. A consolidating institutional apartment landscape narrows the buyer pool for large portfolios but can free up mid-market assets. (via The Promote)

items.headline: RFR buys $1M condo purely to veto SL Green's air-rights deal
items.summary: RFR bought a $1M apartment at 5 E. 44th St. to gain owner status and block SL Green's pending purchase of the building's unused air rights for its 346 Madison assemblage, exploiting the condo board's unanimous-consent rule. SLG paid $160M for the former Brooks Brothers site about a year ago and has since brought in Mori Building as a JV partner. The board meets this week to move to supermajority approval; RFR has sued to void its contract. (via The Promote)

items.headline: 601W's split screen: buying at discounts while defaulting on legacy debt
items.summary: 601W has become one of the most acquisitive national buyers of discounted post-Covid office, taking Wells Fargo Center North in DTLA for $180M ($130/sf) against $500M+ of debt and Durst's 42nd St. tower for $165M at a reported mid-7s cap, across a ~21M sf national portfolio. Simultaneously it defaulted on a $343M Blackstone loan on One South Wacker in Chicago and is seeking a three-year extension on Aon Center debt. The playbook — let legacy basis go, buy the reset — is the defining move of this cycle. (via The Promote)

items.headline: Senior housing occupancy on track for 90% in 2026, 93% by 2028
items.summary: NIC MAP and industry forecasts put senior housing occupancy reaching 90% in 2026 and stabilizing near 93% by 2028, with rent growth normalizing above 4% annually and transaction activity described as robust. Demand is leading and capital is reopening after a constrained 2023–2025 stretch. The constraint shifts from filling units to having units — new development remains well below demographic need.

items.headline: Senior living workforce strategy shifts from shortages to long-term stability
items.summary: McKnight's reports that operators have moved past emergency staffing tactics toward sustainable workforce strategy, focused on the financial burden of competitive compensation and building a caregiver pipeline. While 75% are raising wages and bonuses, 81% are investing in workplace culture, 49% in internal training and upskilling, and 46% in career ladders. Retention spend is diversifying away from pure wage escalation.

items.headline: Ziegler: compensation holds at 56% of senior living operating budgets
items.summary: Ziegler's July 2026 CFO Hotline finds employee compensation averaging 56% of operating budgets year to date, essentially flat versus 2025 — evidence that wage inflation has finally normalized. Still, 62.3% of departing workers cited non-competitive pay as a factor in leaving the industry. Flat comp ratios against rising RevPOR is exactly the margin expansion story driving REIT NOI guidance upgrades.

items.headline: Multifamily rents rose again in July, led by Sun Belt metros
items.summary: Yardi data show average advertised rent up $4, or 0.2%, from June to $1,771, with many Sun Belt metros posting strong monthly gains. After 2025's negative-to-flat rent growth and occupancy in the low 92%–94% range, supply moderation is finally letting pricing power return. High-supply Sun Belt and Mountain markets still face a timeline pushed to late 2026 for durable positive asking-rent growth.

items.headline: Apartment REITs signal growing Sun Belt confidence on Q2 calls
items.summary: Several multifamily REIT leaders — Camden and MAA notably — expressed growing confidence about Sun Belt prospects on Q2 2026 earnings calls as the record supply wave moderates. The narrative has flipped from defense to selective offense in markets that were oversupplied 18 months ago. For Lloyd Jones's Sun Belt exposure, the read-through is that concessions should begin burning off through late 2026.

items.headline: AI phone agents and billing bots start showing hard ROI in senior living
items.summary: Phoenix Senior Living deployed AI phone agents across its 57 communities to guide prospect inquiries, and Bickford Senior Living credits an AI billing-reconciliation system with roughly $1 million in net new annual revenue. Argentum's survey found ~70% of senior living tech and C-suite executives already use AI for predictive analytics, with staff efficiency and resident chatbots close behind. These are back-office wins with measurable payback, not pilots.

items.headline: Providers tell HHS that AI adoption needs infrastructure investment first
items.summary: Provider groups told HHS that AI adoption across aging services is bottlenecked by digital infrastructure gaps — connectivity, data systems and readiness — particularly in assisted living and nursing homes. LeadingAge flagged limited adoption capacity across the care continuum as the core barrier to private-sector innovation. Operators budgeting for AI should assume the first dollars go to plumbing, not algorithms.

items.headline: AI property management adopters project 31% portfolio growth vs 12% for holdouts
items.summary: AI adoption in property management jumped from 20% in 2024 to 58% in 2025, though only 8% of companies have fully automated any single process. Adopters expect 31% portfolio growth in 2026 versus 12% for non-adopters. Analysts peg the total unlock at $430–550 billion in annual value across real estate, construction and development — the gap is execution depth, not experimentation.

items.headline: LAZ-led group takes control of Hartford's distressed Stilts Building
items.summary: An investment group led by parking operator LAZ acquired Hartford's landmark 'Stilts Building' from Shelbourne, ending a foreclosure on the distressed downtown tower. Local operator-led recapitalizations are increasingly the resolution path for secondary-market office distress where institutional bidders have stepped away. (via The Promote)

items.headline: NYC homeowners sue over Mamdani's pied-a-terre tax rollout
items.summary: A group of New York City homeowners filed suit challenging how Mayor Mamdani's pied-a-terre tax on non-primary residences is being implemented. The case injects legal risk into a marquee revenue measure and adds to underwriting uncertainty for NYC residential owners. (via The Promote)

items.headline: 71% of leaders report rising stress; 40% weighing an exit
items.summary: DDI's 2026 leadership research finds 71% of leaders under increased stress, with 40% considering leaving their jobs — a retention risk concentrated in the middle-management layer that actually executes strategy. Meanwhile companies using AI as a strategic partner are growing revenue 1.7x faster than peers, raising the performance bar on already-stretched teams. Leadership bench depth is becoming the binding constraint on growth plans.

items.headline: Global data center buildout accelerates with multibillion-dollar August starts
items.summary: August brought a wave of new data center commitments: ByteDance broke ground on a $38.4B campus at Brazil's Pecém port with 200 MW initial capacity, AWS expanded in Hyderabad under a $48B India plan, and DigitalBridge launched Nippon Gateway Infrastructure with assets acquired from NEC. Power availability, not capital, is now the gating factor. The competition for sites and electricity has direct knock-on effects for land pricing in growth metros.

items.headline: Senior living enters 2026 'at a critical juncture'
items.summary: McKnight's frames 2026 as an inflection point for senior living: demand demographics are undeniable, capital is returning, but development starts remain far below what the 80+ cohort will require. Operators that fix labor stability and technology plumbing now will be positioned when the supply gap becomes acute later this decade.

items.headline: Wellbeing-integrated management linked to 20–25% higher productivity
items.summary: McKinsey Health Institute research finds companies that embed wellbeing into leadership practice, performance management and org design report up to 20–25% higher productivity and measurable reductions in burnout costs. Separately, 90% of employees report burnout symptoms in the past year, nearly 40% at least weekly. In a labor-intensive business like senior living, this is an operating metric, not an HR nicety.

items.headline: 'Emotional fitness' emerges as 2026's defining wellness category
items.summary: Wellhub's State of Work-Life Wellness 2026 finds 89% of employees perform better when prioritizing wellbeing, and employees now weigh wellbeing as heavily as salary. The year's dominant trend is 'emotional fitness' — cognitive performance plus emotional resilience — supported by AI-driven analytics, at-home biomarker tests and richer wearables. Resident-facing wellness programming is the obvious application for senior living operators.

items.headline: CEOs shift from questioning AI to compounding speed with it
items.summary: 2026 CEO research points to a decisive shift: leaders have stopped debating whether AI works and are competing on how fast they can operationalize it, alongside a move from global-default supply chains to portfolios of regional plays. A related trend is the 'People P&L' — tracking growth per individual rather than just revenue per employee. Speed of decision-making is the differentiator leaders are optimizing for.
